summary: Mandarin Chinese (普通话 Pǔtōnghuà, ‘the common speech’) is the standard language of China and Taiwan and has more native speakers than any other language. It is the clearest isolating language of this course: a word never changes its form — no endings for tense, person, number, case or gender. Grammar lives in word order and in small separate words (measure words, particles such as 吗 and 了). Every syllable carries a tone that tells words apart, and the language is written in characters — one character per syllable — with pinyin as the Latin spelling for learners.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Sino-Tibetan › Sinitic (the Chinese languages). Mandarin is the largest Sinitic language; Cantonese, Wu (Shanghainese), Min (Hokkien) and Hakka are sister languages that a Mandarin speaker does not understand without learning them.

facts.label: Script and direction
facts.value: Chinese characters (汉字 hànzì), one per syllable, written left to right in horizontal lines (older and some Taiwanese and Hong Kong texts run in columns, top to bottom, right to left). Simplified characters in mainland China and Singapore, traditional characters in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.

facts.label: Romanization
facts.value: Hanyu Pinyin (adopted in 1958): Latin letters with tone marks — mā, má, mǎ, mà. It is how you look words up and type characters.

facts.label: Standard variety
facts.value: Standard Mandarin — 普通话 in the PRC, 國語 Guóyǔ in Taiwan, 华语 Huáyǔ in Singapore — based on the pronunciation of Beijing and the grammar of northern Mandarin and modern written Chinese.

facts.label: Speakers
facts.value: Roughly 900 million native speakers and over a billion in all (conservative estimates). Official in China, Taiwan and Singapore; one of the six official languages of the United Nations.

typology.why: No word has endings: 我是学生 ‘I am a student’ and 他们是学生 ‘they are students’ — 是 and 学生 never change. Plural, tense, person and case are not marked on words; meaning comes from word order (subject – verb – object), from separate grammar words (们 for groups of people, 了 for completed actions, 吗 for questions) and from context.
typology.alsoShows: Most words are compounds of one-syllable morphemes, much as in German: 电 ‘electricity’ + 话 ‘speech’ = 电话 ‘telephone’, 手 ‘hand’ + 机 ‘machine’ = 手机 ‘mobile phone’. A few suffixes behave a little like agglutination (们 for groups of people, the noun suffixes 子 and 儿), and Chinese is topic-prominent: what you talk about comes first, then what you say about it (这本书我看过 ‘this book, I have read it’).

peculiarities.title: Tones
peculiarities.text: Every syllable has one of four tones or a neutral tone, and the tone is part of the word: 妈 mā ‘mother’, 麻 má ‘hemp’, 马 mǎ ‘horse’, 骂 mà ‘to scold’. Some tones change in combination (你好 is said ní hǎo). Lesson S00 teaches them.

peculiarities.title: Characters, not letters
peculiarities.text: A character stands for a syllable with a meaning, not for a sound. About 3,500 common characters cover more than 99 % of everyday texts; you learn them through the words that contain them, and pinyin tells you how to say them.

peculiarities.title: Words never change
peculiarities.text: No conjugation, no plural ending, no cases, no gender: 我 is both ‘I’ and ‘me’, 书 is ‘book’ and ‘books’, 是 is ‘am, is, are, was, were’. What you learn instead is word order and a set of small grammar words.

peculiarities.title: Measure words
peculiarities.text: Between a number or 这 / 那 and a noun comes a measure word chosen by the kind of thing: 一本书 ‘a book’, 这张桌子 ‘this table’, 三个人 ‘three people’. Every noun is learned with its measure word, as a German noun is learned with its article.

peculiarities.title: 是 links only nouns
peculiarities.text: 是 ‘to be’ joins two nouns (我是老师). Adjectives need no ‘to be’ at all — they work like verbs: 我很好 ‘I am fine’, never *我是好. Being somewhere is 在: 老师在这里 ‘the teacher is here’.

peculiarities.title: No articles, one tā
peculiarities.text: There is no ‘the’ or ‘a’: the place in the sentence and 这 / 那 / 一 + measure word do that work. And ‘he’, ‘she’ and ‘it’ are all tā in speech — 他, 她, 它 differ only in writing.

peculiarities.title: Questions keep the statement order
peculiarities.text: Add 吗 to a statement and it becomes a yes/no question (你是学生吗？); a question word stays where the answer will be (你叫什么名字？). Nothing moves, nothing is inverted.

peculiarities.title: The modifier comes first
peculiarities.text: Everything that describes a noun stands before it, even long phrases: 我的书 ‘my book’; and time and place stand before the verb: 我明天在家吃饭 ‘I eat at home tomorrow’.

forYou.text: Almost everything Greek inflects disappears: no genders, no cases, no verb endings. The new things are tones (the Greek accent is stress, not pitch that changes the word) and measure words. A gift from Greek: Chinese b, d, g are unaspirated like Greek π, τ, κ, while p, t, k are said with a strong puff of air — and Chinese h sounds like Greek χ in χαρά.

The order subject – verb – object is the same as in English (我是学生 = I am a student), and English is already fairly analytic, so the idea of grammar without endings feels natural. Watch out for pinyin letters with un-English values (q, x, zh, c, ü) and for English intonation: in Chinese the pitch belongs to each word, so a question is made with 吗, not by raising the voice.

Your German compounds help a lot: Chinese builds words the same way (手机 ‘hand machine’ — the German Handy; 电话 ‘electric speech’). German ü is pinyin ü (女 nǚ), German ach-Laut is close to Chinese h, the ich-Laut close to x. Measure words have small German cousins — ein Blatt Papier, eine Tasse Kaffee, zwei Stück Kuchen — but in Chinese every counted noun needs one. Forget V2: the Chinese verb never moves to second place (明天我去 or 我明天去, never *明天去我).

Like Russian, Chinese has no articles. Russian drops ‘to be’ in the present (Я студент); Chinese needs 是 between two nouns (我是学生) but, like Russian, uses none before adjectives (她很高 ~ Она высокая). Russian ш is close to Chinese sh, щ to x, and your feel for verbal aspect (perfective / imperfective) will help with 了 and 过 later.

Turkish is the opposite technique — long words built from suffixes — yet many habits carry over: no gender (Turkish o = he/she/it, just like spoken tā), no articles (bir works like 一 + measure word), no plural after a number (iki kitap ~ 两本书), and modifiers before the noun. Turkish ü and the idea of a fixed word order help; the difference is that Chinese puts the verb before the object (SVO), Turkish at the end.

pathNote: Chinese walks the same 19 steps as Arabic, Hebrew and German, but as an isolating language it never learns endings or tables — at each step it learns word order and small grammar words instead. S00 the tones (with the overview). S01 是 links nouns only; 在 is ‘to be somewhere’. S02 你 / 您 — no forms ‘to a man / to a woman’. S03 measure words after 这 / 那 (这本书). S04 no gender and no articles: Chinese shows what it does instead. S05 numbers with measure words, 两 / 二, and no plural (们 only for people). S06 有 for ‘have’ and 的 for ‘my, your’ (dropped with close family: 我妈妈), with the paternal and maternal family words. S07 verbs that never change and the fixed order subject – verb – object. S08 the two negations 不 / 没. S09 questions with 吗, A-not-A and 还是. S10 question words that stay in place. S11 coverbs before the verb (在, 从, 跟, 给) instead of cases. S12 place words after the noun (桌子上). S13 去 / 来, 从…到, travel with 坐 / 骑 before the verb, and commands with 请, 吧 and 别. S14 time before the verb and the aspect particles 了 / 过 (在 for ‘in progress’). S15 no word for ‘at / on / in’ a time; 以前 / 以后 / 的时候 after the clause; dates from big to small. S16 adjectives used like verbs — 很 instead of 是, 的 before a noun. S17 comparison with 比, 更, 最, 没有 and 一样 — the adjective never changes. S18 paired linking words (因为…所以, 虽然…但是, 如果…就), …的时候 after its clause, and no word for ‘that’. Where the fusional languages learn conjugation and declension tables, Chinese learns word order and small grammar words.

blocks.title: The one-sentence model
blocks.text: Chinese = fixed word order + small grammar words + tones; the words themselves never change.

quiz.q: Which morphological type is Mandarin Chinese?
quiz.why: Words never change their form; grammar is word order and separate small words.

quiz.q: What tells 妈 mā ‘mother’ from 马 mǎ ‘horse’?
quiz.why: Same syllable ma, different tone: 1st (high level) vs 3rd (low dipping).

quiz.q: How do you say ‘I am fine’?
quiz.why: Adjectives take no 是; 很 links them to the subject.

quiz.q: What stands between a number and a noun?
quiz.why: 一本书 ‘a book’, 三个人 ‘three people’.

quiz.q: Which characters are used in mainland China?
quiz.why: Mainland China and Singapore use simplified characters; Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau traditional ones.

quiz.q: How many ways are there to say ‘he’, ‘she’ and ‘it’ in speech?
quiz.why: 他, 她 and 它 are all pronounced tā; they differ only in writing.

quiz.q: How do you turn 你是学生 into a yes/no question?
quiz.why: 你是学生吗？ — the statement order stays.

seeAlso.note: German is fusional: gender, four cases and conjugation tables — everything Chinese does without.
Arabic builds words from three-consonant roots and has no ‘to be’ in the present; Chinese builds words by compounding and needs 是 between nouns.
Hebrew shares the Semitic roots and the verbless present with Arabic; like Chinese it puts no ‘to be’ before adjectives.
